title: COMPUTING MACHINERY
body:
The first course that goes underneath the language. First year taught you to write programs;
this one shows you what the machine actually does with them: how a [[CPU]] fetches and
executes, how numbers and characters are really stored, and what an instruction looks like
when there is no compiler left to hide it. Everything is taught on the [[Motorola 68000]],
so [[Assembly]] here is concrete rather than abstract.

It sits directly below [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE 2]], where the [[Pointer]]s and
[[Memory]] layout you took on faith in C become addresses and registers here, and it feeds
straight into [[COMPUTING MACHINERY 2]] (digital logic and I/O) and then [[OPERATING SYSTEMS]].

## Topics

### The machine

[[Computer Architecture]] · [[Motorola 68000]] · [[VonNeumann]] · [[CPU]] · [[Bus]] ·
[[Main memory]] · [[Cache]] · [[Clock]]

The 68000 is a [[VonNeumann]] machine: one memory holding both instructions and data, one
[[Bus]] to reach it. The [[CPU]] splits into a control unit, an [[ALU]], and registers:
data registers, address registers, the PC, and the [[Status Register]] whose [[Status Bits]]
are how instructions talk back to you.

Support chips around the processor: [[6850 ACIA]] (keyboard), [[68901 MFP]] (the [[PIC]]),
[[YM2149]] (the [[PSG]]), and [[GLUE]], the system controller. All four come back in
[[COMPUTING MACHINERY 2]].

### Data representation

[[Data representation]] · [[Integer Representation]] · [[Character Representation]] ·
[[Boolean Representation]] · [[Base Conversion]] · [[Complements]] · [[ASCII]]

How a [[Data type]] you declared in C is actually laid out in bits. [[Base Conversion]]
between binary, octal, decimal, and hex is the working skill; [[Complements]] (two's
complement) is how the same adder handles subtraction. [[ASCII]] is the character encoding
the 68000 assumes.

### Assembly programming

[[Assembly]] · [[Instructions]] · [[Directives]] · [[Addressing Modes]] ·
[[Branching and Looping]] · [[Subroutines]] · [[Assembly Errors]]

[[Instructions]] do the work, [[Directives]] tell the assembler things, and
[[Addressing Modes]] decide where an operand actually comes from:

| Mode | Written as | Operand is |
|---|---|---|
| Register direct | `d0`, `a1` | the register's contents |
| Immediate | `#5` | the literal value, never valid as a destination |
| Absolute | `5`, `var` | the value stored *at* that address |
| Register indirect | `(a0)` | the value the register points at, i.e. dereferencing |

[[Branching and Looping]] is control flow once `if` and `while` are gone: `cmp` sets the
[[Status Bits]], a conditional branch reads them, and `dbra` counts down. [[Subroutines]] is
`jsr` / `rts` plus the stack discipline that makes arguments, locals, and [[Recursion]] work.

### Errors and error detection

[[Assembly Errors]] · [[Error Detection]]

Errors sort by *when* they bite: assembly time (syntax), link time (unresolved references),
run-time behavioural ([[Logic Errors]]), and run-time faults, the ones that crash. The
68000 detects bus errors, address errors, illegal instructions, and privilege violations in
hardware, and each shows a different bomb count.

### Where the operating system starts

[[Operating System]] · [[Kernel]] · [[System Call]]

The privilege boundary shows up at the end of this course and becomes the whole subject of
[[OPERATING SYSTEMS]]. A [[System Call]] is how a user-mode program asks the [[Kernel]] for
something it is not allowed to do itself, and a privilege violation is what happens when it
tries anyway.

### Maths on the machine

[[Mathematical Operations]] · [[Binary Operations]]

## Core Facts to Know

- The [[Motorola 68000]] is a [[VonNeumann]] machine: instructions and data share one memory.
- The [[CPU]] is a control unit, an [[ALU]], and registers.
- The 68000 has separate data registers (`d0`–`d7`) and address registers (`a0`–`a7`).
- The [[Status Register]] holds the [[Status Bits]].
- [[Status Bits]] are the *indirect* result of an instruction; you don't ask for them, you get them.
- Number literals are prefixed `$` for hex, `@` for octal, `%` for binary; no prefix means decimal.
- Instruction size suffixes are `.b` (byte), `.w` (word), `.l` (longword).
- The four [[Addressing Modes]] are register direct, immediate, absolute, and register indirect.
- Immediate is never a valid *destination*.
- Register indirect `(a0)` is the assembly equivalent of dereferencing a [[Pointer]].
- `move` copies; `clr` is the same as moving 0 to the destination.
- For `add`, either the source or the destination must be a data register.
- `adda` is add-address: it takes address registers, not data registers.
- `ext` sign-extends a value to a larger size.
- Subtraction is destination − source, or destination + the two's [[Complements|complement]] of source.
- Carry is the unsigned overflow flag; V is the signed one. The hardware sets both, you pick.
- `cmp d1,d0` is a `sub` that keeps only the flags: it computes `d0 - d1`, so operand order reads backwards.
- Signed branches are `bgt`/`blt`; unsigned are `bhi`/`bcs`. Mixing them up assembles fine and is wrong.
- `dbra` branches while the counter is **not −1**, so an $n$-iteration loop starts at $n-1$.
- `jsr` pushes the return address, `rts` pops it. Everything else about a call is convention.
- The stack grows downwards: `-(sp)` pushes, `(sp)+` pops. `a7` is `sp`.
- `dc` emits bytes, `ds` reserves space, `equ` names a value and emits nothing.
- `even` after byte data is what stops the next word access being an address error.
- Assembly-time errors are syntax; link-time errors are unresolved external references.
- A **bus error** (2 bombs) is an access outside addressable memory or to a protected address.
- An **address error** (3 bombs) is a word or longword access at an *odd* address.
- An **illegal instruction** (4 bombs) is executing data as code, usually after a stray jump.
- A **privilege violation** (8 bombs) is running a supervisor-only instruction from user mode.
- The [[CPU]] does not know which addresses are protected; that is the operating system's problem.
- [[ASCII]] is a 7-bit character encoding.
- The [[6850 ACIA]] is the keyboard controller chip.
- The [[68901 MFP]] is the [[PIC]] on the 68000, and is smart enough to do vector transfer.
- The [[YM2149]] is the [[PSG]], the sound chip.
- [[GLUE]] is the system controller.
- [[Cache]] exists because [[Main memory]] is slower than the [[CPU]].
- ROM is read-only; RAM is what the CPU reads and writes at speed.

## Related courses

- [[COMPUTING MACHINERY 2]], the direct sequel. What is *inside* the [[CPU]]
  ([[Digital Logic]], [[Combinational Logic]], [[Sequential Logic]]) and how it talks to the
  world ([[I-O]], [[Interrupts]], [[Direct Memory Access]]).
- [[OPERATING SYSTEMS]]: picks up [[Kernel]], [[System Call]], [[Supervisor State]],
  [[Main memory]], and [[Cache]] and builds a whole course on them.
- [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE 2]], the [[C]] side of the same story: [[Memory]], [[Pointer]],
  [[Stack and Heap]], [[Byte]], [[Type casting]]. This course explains why those work.
- [[INTRODUCTION TO SOFTWARE ENGINEERING]]: the [[Assembly Errors]] taxonomy is the same
  compile / link / run-time split you meet again as [[Compile Errors]], [[Logic Errors]],
  and [[Runtime Errors]].
- [[DISCRETE MATH]]: [[Base Conversion]] and [[Boolean Representation]] are the applied
  half of number bases and boolean logic.
